specPoints.text: understand the reasons for the trends in thermal stability of the nitrates and the carbonates of the elements in Groups 1 and 2 in terms of the size and charge of the cations involved

primer.text: Heat a Group 1 or 2 carbonate or nitrate and it cracks apart - but how easily depends on the cation above it. Small, doubly charged ions distort the big negative ions and trigger earlier decomposition. This note gives the decomposition equations for both anion families and finishes with the gas tests that identify the products.

lessons.title: Carbonates under heat
lessons.opening: Thermal decomposition breaks a compound apart with heat, and the carbonate family splits cleanly: lithium stands alone in Group 1, while every Group 2 carbonate yields oxide plus carbon dioxide. This lesson writes the equations and tracks the heat bill downward.
keyPoints: Thermal decomposition uses heat to split one compound into several fresh substances.
Lithium carbonate decomposes to lithium oxide and carbon dioxide; the other Group 1 carbonates hold at Bunsen temperatures.
Group 2 carbonates decompose as XCO3 -> XO + CO2.
Magnesium carbonate is the classic example: MgCO3 -> MgO + CO2.
More heat is needed for decomposition as you descend both groups.

low.restatement: Heat cracks the carbonate into an oxide and carbon dioxide gas; lithium is the only Group 1 member fragile enough to crack, and every step down either group raises the temperature bill.
low.analogy: A row of sandcastles of increasing firmness: the smallest castle (lithium) crumbles first, and each larger one needs a stronger wave (more heat).
low.examPointer: Name the products with states - solid oxide plus gaseous CO2 - and flag lithium's uniqueness inside Group 1.

medium.restatement: Decomposition demands polarising the carbonate ion apart; the small Li+ and small 2+ cations at the group tops distort the anion most, so their salts crack at the lowest temperatures while the large cations below shield their carbonates.
medium.analogy: A balloon squeezed between fingers: small strong fingers (high polarising power) pop it easily; broad mittens (large cations) merely cradle it.
medium.examPointer: Write the general Group 2 equation with X - XCO3 -> XO + CO2 - before quoting specific members in answers.

check.stem: Which Group 1 carbonate decomposes at Bunsen temperatures?

options.explanation: Li2CO3 cracks to Li2O and CO2.
It holds firm at Bunsen temperatures.
It is even more stable than sodium's.
Lithium's is the exception that does crack.

check.stem: What are the products of Group 2 carbonate decomposition?

options.text: The metal oxide and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: XCO3 -> XO + CO2.
No water participates in the decomposition.
That is the nitrate family.
Carbonates never reduce that far.

check.stem: How does the decomposition temperature trend down Group 2?

options.text: More heat is needed going down
options.explanation: Larger cations protect their carbonates.

options.text: Less heat is needed going down
options.explanation: The bill climbs, not falls.
The temperatures clearly differ.
Every Group 2 carbonate decomposes with enough heat.

check.stem: Why does lithium carbonate decompose while sodium carbonate does not?

options.text: Lithium's small cation polarises the carbonate ion more strongly
options.explanation: High polarising power destabilises the anion.
Mass does not set stability.
Both are ionic salts.
It is an anhydrous salt.

check.stem: What general equation covers the Group 2 carbonates?

options.explanation: One carbonate yields one oxide plus one CO2.
No such cleavage occurs.
The per-formula equation is the general form.
Water plays no role here.

check.stem: Write the equation for lithium carbonate's decomposition.
State what happens to the decomposition temperatures down both groups.
check.modelAnswer: The decomposition temperatures increase going down both groups, so more heat is needed for the heavier members.

check.stem: Explain why small cations destabilise carbonates more than large ones.
check.modelAnswer: A small, highly charged cation polarises the carbonate ion, drawing its delocalised electrons toward itself and weakening the anion's internal bonds, so the carbonate cracks apart at lower temperature.

check.stem: Magnesium carbonate decomposes per MgCO3 -> MgO + CO2. What mass of CO2 (M = 44) escapes from 8.4 g of MgCO3 (M = 84)?
check.modelAnswer: 8.4 g is 0.1 mol of carbonate, releasing 0.1 mol of CO2, which is 4.4 g.

lessons.title: Nitrates under heat and the gas tests
lessons.opening: Nitrates split three ways: lithium alone gives NO2, the sodium-to-caesium run gives nitrites, and Group 2 gives oxide, NO2 and oxygen. This lesson writes all three equations, explains the same polarising reason, and closes with the gas tests.
keyPoints: The rest of Group 1 decomposes to the metal nitrite and oxygen: 2XNO3 -> 2XNO2 + O2.
Group 2 nitrates decompose to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, as Mg(NO3)2 -> MgO + 2NO2 + 1/2 O2.
Nitrogen dioxide's toxicity sends nitrate decompositions to the fume cupboard.
Limewater tests CO2, a glowing splint tests O2, and NO2 dissolves to acidic products.

low.restatement: Heat the nitrate and watch the products: lithium behaves like Group 2, the middle alkali metals stop at nitrites, and Group 2 always gives the brown NO2 gas - handle it in the fume cupboard.
low.analogy: Three exit doors from the same room: lithium and Group 2 take the full-decomposition door, the heavier alkalis take the nitrite door, and the brown smoke marks the NO2 exit.
low.examPointer: Balance the Group 2 nitrate equation carefully - the half-oxygen coefficient is correct per formula unit: Mg(NO3)2 -> MgO + 2NO2 + 1/2 O2.

medium.restatement: The same polarising argument runs the nitrate family: small cations distort NO3- enough to push all the way to NO2, while large cations only manage the nitrite; the gas tests then fingerprint the products - limewater for CO2, splint for O2, acidic brown fumes for NO2.
medium.analogy: Ripeness scales with squeezing: a firm squeeze (small cation) yields juice all the way (NO2), a gentle grip (large cation) yields only a little (nitrite).
medium.examPointer: Write the limewater equation with states: Ca(OH)2 (aq) + CO2 (g) -> CaCO3 (s) + H2O (l) - the milky precipitate is the answer.

check.stem: Which products form when lithium nitrate decomposes?

options.text: Lithium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen
options.explanation: The full decomposition mirrors Group 2.
That is the heavier Group 1 route.
No carbonate appears.
The gas is NO2, not NO.

options.text: The decomposition of Group 1 nitrates from sodium to caesium
options.explanation: The nitrite-plus-oxygen route belongs to the middle alkali metals.
Group 2 goes all the way to the oxide plus NO2.
Lithium takes the full route.
The three routes differ.

check.stem: Why are nitrate decompositions carried out in a fume cupboard?

options.text: Nitrogen dioxide is a toxic brown gas
options.explanation: The fume cupboard carries it away.
Oxygen release is a hazard but not the named reason.
No radioactivity is involved.
The named hazard is the NO2.

check.stem: What does carbon dioxide do to limewater?

options.text: Turns it milky through fine calcium carbonate precipitate
options.explanation: The white suspension is the positive test.
Blue belongs to litmus in alkali.
The CO2 is absorbed, not decomposed.
The milky turn is textbook.
The reigniting splint is the oxygen fingerprint.
That is CO2's test.
Oxygen is odourless.
That marks acidic gases.

check.stem: Write the equation for thermal decomposition of lithium nitrate.
State the gas test for nitrogen dioxide's acidity.
check.modelAnswer: Dissolved in water, NO2 gives an acidic solution, forming 2HNO3 plus HNO2 from 2NO2 + H2O.

check.stem: Explain why the same polarising argument covers both carbonates and nitrates.
check.modelAnswer: Both anions are large, delocalised species; small cations distort either one, so thermal stability rises down both groups for the same physical reason.

check.stem: Balance the full-integer form of magnesium nitrate's decomposition: Mg(NO3)2 -> MgO + 2NO2 + ?O2.
check.modelAnswer: The oxygen census 6 = 1 + 4 + 1 fixes the last coefficient at 1/2, or doubled: 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2.

glossary.definition: The splitting of a compound into fresh substances using heat.
The ability of a small, highly charged cation to distort a nearby anion's electron cloud and weaken it.
The NO2- ion, the partial-decomposition product of most Group 1 nitrates.
